name: Spring onion
summary: How Filipino growers raise spring onion for its green leaves, from small bulbs or from seed, on beds near markets and on highland farms. Whole plants are pulled in about seven weeks, or the leaves are cut so they grow back.
season: Grown all year where there is water. It is easier in the dry months, since long heavy rain rots the plants. Highland farms grow it the year round.
material: Small bulbs of the native sibuyas tagalog type, split into single bulbs with the tops trimmed off, or seed of bunching onion sown in a seedbed and transplanted after about a month.
spacing: Raised beds about a meter wide, bulbs about 10 to 15 cm apart each way.
water: Watered by hand or from a canal every morning in the first week, then every one to two days in dry weather. Beds must drain well in the rains.
fertilizer: Plenty of dried manure or compost in the beds, then urea (46 0 0) or complete fertilizer (14 14 14) side dressed twice, often dissolved in water.
care: Frequent hand weeding, steady watering, and watching for armyworm, thrips and leaf rot in wet weather.
harvest: Whole plants are pulled at about 45 to 50 days, or leaves are cut for regrowth. They are washed, bundled and sold fresh.

steps.title: Make the beds
steps.how: Dig or plow the plot and make raised beds about a meter wide. Mix in plenty of dried manure or compost.

steps.title: Prepare the bulbs
steps.how: Split the clumps into single bulbs and cut off the top part of each bulb so it sprouts faster.

steps.title: Plant the bulbs
steps.how: Push the bulbs into the bed about 10 to 15 cm apart each way, with the cut top just at the surface. Water the bed.

steps.title: Water daily at first
steps.how: Water every morning in the first week, then every one to two days if there is no rain.

steps.title: Weed
steps.how: Hand pull the weeds on the beds.

steps.title: Feed
steps.how: Side dress urea (46 0 0) or complete fertilizer (14 14 14) between the plants and water it in. Some growers dissolve the fertilizer in the watering can.

steps.title: Watch for armyworm and thrips
steps.how: Check the leaves for small caterpillars, egg masses and silvery streaks from thrips.

steps.title: Second feeding
steps.how: Give another light side dressing of urea and water it in.

steps.title: Pull or cut
steps.how: Pull whole plants at about 45 to 50 days when the leaves are full and green, or cut the leaves above the base so they grow back for another cutting.

steps.title: Wash and bundle
steps.how: Wash off the soil, trim the roots and old leaves, tie in bundles and sell fresh the same day.

mistakes: Planting in beds that hold water, so the bulbs rot in the rains.
Letting the beds dry out, which gives thin, tough leaves.
Using bulbs from a diseased crop, which carries the disease along.
better: Use clean, firm bulbs or fresh seed.
Raise the beds and add compost so they drain and hold moisture.
Feed little and often, and water in the mornings.
Plant in batches every couple of weeks for a steady supply.

watering.traditional: Spring onion is watered often because its roots are short. Growers water by hand with a can or a hose, or let water from a canal into the beds, every morning in the first week and every one to two days after that in dry weather.
watering.method: Hand watering with a can or a hose, or letting canal water into the furrows between beds. Water in the early morning.
watering.rainfed: In the rainy months the rain does most of the watering, but plant on raised beds and water in any dry spell. It is not grown on rain alone in the dry months.
watering.dryseason: Water every one to two days, and every day in the hottest weeks or on sandy soil. Water when the top of the bed is dry or the leaf tips turn yellow.
watering.wet: Long heavy rain rots the plants, so keep the beds raised and the paths open for drainage, and skip watering on rainy days.

schedule.amount: Enough to wet the bed through, gently so the bulbs are not washed out
schedule.why: The cut bulbs need moisture to root and sprout fast.

schedule.often: Every one to two days in dry weather, and right after each feeding
schedule.amount: Wet the bed to a finger deep or more, with no water left standing
schedule.why: Steady moisture gives long, tender, green leaves.

schedule.often: Keep watering as before, and water the day before pulling
schedule.why: Moist soil makes pulling easy and keeps the leaves fresh.

critical: The first week: the bulbs must not dry out while they root.
All through leaf growth: dry beds give tough, yellow tipped leaves.

signs.dry: Leaf tips turn yellow and dry, leaves stay short and tough, and the plants bend over.
signs.wet: Leaves yellow and go soft, and the bulbs and roots rot.

better: A thin rice straw mulch on the beds keeps the soil moist and the leaves clean.
A sprinkler or drip line on bigger beds gives even water with less work.
